Groningen
groh'ning-en
n. (city and province of the northern Netherlands; taken for the Republic in 1594 and reformed thereafter)
From Middle Dutch Groeningen, perhaps the people of Groni, or the green place.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Groningen came late. While Holland and Zeeland had been Reformed for twenty years, the city and its Ommelanden stayed under Spanish control, and the Reformation reached them only when Prince Maurice took the place by siege in July 1594; the Reduction of Groningen brought the province into the Republic, and a university followed in 1614. Francis Gomarus, who would oppose Arminius at Leiden and shape the Canons of Dort, was a native of the city, born there in 1563 while it was still Catholic. The dictionary records Groningen because the delay is instructive. God gives a city its visitation in His own time, and the twenty-year gap between Holland and Groningen was not a failure of the gospel but a difference of appointment. “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1), and the waiting is commanded with the promise: “though it tarry, wait for it” (Hab 2:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines time as a particular portion of duration, patience as endurance without murmuring, and longsuffering as bearing provocation for a long time and not easily provoked.

expand to see more

TIME, n. 1. A particular portion or part of duration, whether past, present or future. The time was; the time has been; the time is; the time will be.

PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.

LONGSUFFERING, a. Bearing injuries or provocation for a long time; patient; not easily provoked.

PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.

Modern Corruption

The northern city taken by Maurice in 1594, reformed twenty years after Holland, and the birthplace of Gomarus.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the impatience that measures the gospel's success by the calendar, so that a region slow to receive it is written off, and a work twenty years behind its neighbours is judged to have failed. Groningen was twenty years behind Holland and produced Gomarus.

The principle to recover is that God appoints the times of visitation, and that waiting for an appointed thing is obedience rather than resignation. The seasons are fixed: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1). Delay is written into the promise itself: “the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry” (Hab 2:3). The mercy has its hour: “for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come” (Psa 102:13). And what looks like slackness is longsuffering: “The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness” (2Pe 3:9).

Usage

"“To every thing there is a season” (Ecc 3:1) — the Reduction of Groningen, July 1594."

"“though it tarry, wait for it” (Hab 2:3) — twenty years behind Holland and Zeeland."

"“the set time, is come” (Psa 102:13) — a university in 1614, and Gomarus born in the city in 1563."
